For \(k=0,1,\dots,4\), let \(P(k)\) be the probability of eventually seeing all 5 primes before a non-prime, given \(k\) distinct primes have already appeared.

From state \(k\):
- Roll a new prime: probability \(\frac{5-k}{12}\), move to \(k+1\).
- Roll an already-seen prime: probability \(\frac{k}{12}\), stay at \(k\).
- Roll a non-prime: probability \(\frac{7}{12}\), failure.

Thus:
\[
P(k)=\frac{5-k}{12}P(k+1)+\frac{k}{12}P(k)
\]
\[
\left(1-\frac{k}{12}\right)P(k)=\frac{5-k}{12}P(k+1)
\]
\[
P(k)=\frac{5-k}{12-k}P(k+1)
\]
with \(P(5)=1\).

Therefore:
\[
P(4)=\frac{1}{8}
\]
\[
P(3)=\frac{2}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{8}=\frac{1}{36}
\]
\[
P(2)=\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{36}=\frac{1}{120}
\]
\[
P(1)=\frac{4}{11}\cdot \frac{1}{120}=\frac{1}{330}
\]
\[
P(0)=\frac{5}{12}\cdot \frac{1}{330}=\frac{1}{792}
\]

So \(p=1\), \(q=792\), and
\[
p+q=\boxed{793}
\]
